title: High blood pressure (hypertension)
text: Hypertension means blood pressure is persistently higher than normal, commonly defined as 130/80 mmHg or above in many current guidelines. It often causes no symptoms, which is why regular blood pressure checks are important. Untreated high blood pressure increases the risk of heart attack, stroke and kidney disease. Lifestyle measures such as reducing salt intake, regular physical activity, limiting alcohol, not smoking and maintaining a healthy weight can lower blood pressure. A doctor may recommend medication if lifestyle changes are not enough.

title: Type 2 diabetes
text: Type 2 diabetes is a condition in which the body does not use insulin effectively, leading to high blood sugar. Common symptoms include increased thirst, frequent urination, tiredness and blurred vision, although many people have no symptoms early on. It is diagnosed with blood tests such as HbA1c or fasting glucose. Management includes healthy eating, physical activity, weight management and, when needed, medicines prescribed by a doctor. Regular check-ups help prevent complications affecting the eyes, kidneys, nerves and heart.

title: Fever in adults
text: A fever is a body temperature of 38°C (100.4°F) or higher and is usually a sign that the body is fighting an infection. Resting and drinking plenty of fluids helps the body recover. Seek medical advice if a fever lasts more than three days, is 39.4°C (103°F) or higher, or comes with a stiff neck, confusion, a rash that does not fade when pressed, difficulty breathing or chest pain.

title: Headache warning signs
text: Most headaches, such as tension-type headaches, are not dangerous and improve with rest, fluids and over-the-counter pain relief used as directed. Get emergency help for a sudden, severe headache that feels like the worst headache of your life. Also seek urgent care if a headache comes with fever and stiff neck, confusion, weakness, vision loss, difficulty speaking or follows a head injury.

title: Chest pain
text: Chest pain can have many causes, including muscle strain, acid reflux and heart problems. Chest pain that feels like pressure, squeezing or tightness, or that spreads to the arm, jaw, neck or back, can be a sign of a heart attack. Other warning signs include shortness of breath, sweating, nausea and light-headedness. Anyone with these symptoms should call emergency services immediately rather than waiting to see if it passes.

title: Stroke warning signs (FAST)
text: A stroke is a medical emergency in which blood supply to part of the brain is interrupted. The FAST test helps recognise it: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency services. Other signs include sudden numbness on one side of the body, sudden confusion, sudden trouble seeing and sudden loss of balance. Fast treatment greatly improves the chances of recovery.

title: Dehydration
text: Dehydration happens when the body loses more fluid than it takes in, for example through vomiting, diarrhoea, sweating or not drinking enough. Signs include thirst, dark yellow urine, passing little urine, dizziness, dry mouth and tiredness. Drinking water or oral rehydration solution usually helps mild dehydration. Seek medical help if someone cannot keep fluids down, is very drowsy or confused, or has not passed urine for many hours.

title: Common cold
text: The common cold is a viral infection of the nose and throat. Symptoms include a runny or blocked nose, sore throat, sneezing and cough, and usually improve within 7 to 10 days. Antibiotics do not work against viruses and are not helpful for a cold. Rest, fluids and symptom relief are the main treatment. See a doctor if symptoms last longer than three weeks, get much worse, or you have difficulty breathing.

title: Asthma
text: Asthma is a long-term condition in which the airways become inflamed and narrow, causing wheezing, shortness of breath, chest tightness and coughing. Common triggers include allergens, smoke, cold air, exercise and respiratory infections. Treatment usually involves inhalers prescribed by a doctor, along with a personal asthma action plan. An asthma attack where a reliever inhaler does not help, or where the person is too breathless to speak, needs emergency care.

title: Migraine
text: A migraine is a type of headache, often a throbbing pain on one side of the head, that can last from hours to days. It may come with nausea, vomiting and sensitivity to light or sound. Some people experience an aura, such as flashing lights or zigzag lines, before the headache. Keeping a headache diary can help identify triggers like poor sleep, stress, certain foods or skipped meals. A doctor can advise on treatments to relieve attacks and on preventive options.

title: Anaphylaxis (severe allergic reaction)
text: Anaphylaxis is a severe, potentially life-threatening allergic reaction that can develop within minutes. Signs include swelling of the throat or tongue, difficulty breathing or swallowing, wheezing, a sudden rash, feeling faint and collapse. It is an emergency: call emergency services immediately. People who have been prescribed an adrenaline (epinephrine) auto-injector should use it as instructed.

title: High cholesterol
text: Cholesterol is a fatty substance in the blood, and high levels of LDL cholesterol can build up in the arteries and raise the risk of heart disease and stroke. High cholesterol usually causes no symptoms and is found with a blood test. Eating less saturated fat, eating more fibre, being physically active, not smoking and limiting alcohol can help lower cholesterol. A doctor may also recommend medication depending on overall cardiovascular risk.

title: Healthy sleep
text: Most adults need about 7 to 9 hours of sleep per night. Keeping a regular sleep schedule, limiting caffeine later in the day, reducing screen use before bed and keeping the bedroom dark and quiet can improve sleep. Ongoing trouble sleeping, loud snoring with pauses in breathing, or excessive daytime sleepiness should be discussed with a doctor.

title: Anxiety
text: Anxiety is a feeling of worry, nervousness or unease that everyone experiences at times. When anxiety is intense, persistent and interferes with daily life, it may be an anxiety disorder, which is common and treatable. Physical symptoms can include a racing heart, rapid breathing, restlessness and trouble sleeping. Talking therapies, lifestyle changes and sometimes medication can help, and a doctor or mental health professional can advise on options. Anyone having thoughts of harming themselves should contact emergency services or a crisis line right away.
